chunks: "The main rules I follow:. One, keep it short. The ISR delays everything of lower or equal priority, so do the minimum, like grab the byte, timestamp, clear the flag, and get out.
A good target is a few microseconds. Two, clear the interrupt flag correctly, and only the flags I handled, otherwise it re-fires forever or I lose an event. Three, never block.
No delays, no waiting on flags, no mutexes, no printf or malloc. They're slow, non-reentrant, or can deadlock. Four, handle shared data carefully.
Anything shared with main is volatile, updates are atomic or in a short critical section, and I prefer one writer per variable and a ring buffer for streams.
Five, defer the real work. The ISR sets a flag or posts to a queue, and main or a task does the parsing, maths and printing. Six, think about priority and stack.
The most time-critical interrupt gets the highest priority, and I budget stack for the worst nested case.
Seven, avoid floating point and big local arrays in ISRs, since they enlarge the frame and take time. And finally, measure it.
I toggle a GPIO at ISR entry and exit and look at the worst case on a scope under load, because ISR timing bugs only show up in the worst case."
